content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper provides an extension to PAC-Bayes theory that applies to reinforcement learning. Their method, PB-LRL supposedly allows lifelong learning agents to optimize a good prior policy distribution, without expert knowledge of environments. Generalisation bounds are provided for their theory.

Experiments were carried out in both discrete and continuous control settings from OpenAI gym, and Mujuco.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- Using larger than usual (10) number of seeds was nice to see.
- Decent introduction to PAC-Bayes for Supervised Learning.


### Weaknesses
- Is it worrying that in Figures 1 and 3, that none of the reward curves leveled off? Were the tasks solved?
- Since this method was based heavily on previous work, could this have been used as a baseline?
- Why was MAML chosen as a baseline here? That work is nearly 5 years old; are there no newer methods that could be used here?
- In the experiments, how varied were the goals? 
- A key point of this paper was to identify that the policy would have a prior that is useful for most tasks in the space of tasks. This didn't seem to be explicitly tested, and I don't think that the experiments necessarily show case this. 
- Is the main difference between this method, and methods of MAML the objective?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
- What LRL stands for isn't mentinoed before it is used (Page 1, 3rd paragraph).
- Could the algorithm have been written out in the main text? If tight for space, a paragraph describing it would have been nice.
- The list in Section 3.2 seems to have overlapping text.


### Quality
- This paper could use another proof-reading review. There are capitalisation issues, as well as grammatical errors in places.

### Novelty
- It looks like this work builds from others, which seem to be referenced. I haven't seen this particular methods before, to the best of my knowledge. 

### Reproducibility
Code is made available.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of lifelong reinforcement learning. The goal is to learn and finetune policies that are capable of performing well on a variety of tasks. This paper takes a PAC-Bayes approach in which a posterior distribution over policies is updated based on observed tasks. Policies are sampled from the posterior and then fine tuned on the task sampled from a fixed distribution. Several PAC-Bayes bounds are shown concerning this setup. Experiments show the method is effective compared to MAML.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The problem is well motivated and interesting, as evidenced by the many papers that exist on this topic.
- The PAC-Bayes application to this particular problem setting appears to be new.
- The experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is very effective in the constructed tasks

Weaknesses:
- I believe it is inaccurate to call this lifelong learning. Typically in lifelong learning, one assumes that the task distribution is non-stationary and thus one is truly trying to optimize for good performance against a changing target. In this paper, the task distribution is fixed. This is more like multi-task or meta RL
- Both multi-task and meta RL are very active and popular fields yet there is very little discussion of them in the related work. Furthermore, many existing algorithms are designed to work precisely in this setting (for a fixed distribution, some for non-stationary distribution), such as RL^2, PEARL, VariBAD. These seem like important and standard baselines that were left out of the empirical evaluations. PEARL and VariBAD also boast significant improvements over MAML for these types of tasks and were evaluated on more mujoco environments.
- It is also not entirely clear how the proposed approach is different from the “baseline” multi-task learning algorithm often used in papers such as [1]. Besides taking the Bayesian approach in which distribution is learned instead of an particular policy, they seem to be very similar.
- Although they are used as motivation, the theoretical results do not appear to be particularly novel. However, the application to this problem setting may be new. Theorem 2 appears to be a standard generalization bound. Theorem 4 lacks details and interpretability. For instance, it is assumed that $\theta_*$ is optimal (w.r.t some unclear objective, see next section) but is also output by the algorithm, but this does not seem to answer the question of whether Alg 1 actually is able to converge to or output $\theta_*$ in the end. It’s unclear whether the theory justifies what the algorithm is trying to achieve.

[1] On the Effectiveness of Fine-tuning Versus Meta-reinforcement Learning
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The notation is inconsistent and confusing. For example, $\pi \sim P$ is used and so is $\theta \sim P$. It is not defined what $\theta$ is (policy parameters, policy outputs for states?). Similarly, $\mu^*$ and $\sigma^*$ are supposedly from the optimal distribution, but what is the objective for which they are optimal?
- The Alg 1, which is a major contribution, and important definitions that are used throughout the paper have been relegated to the appendix.
- C(\Tau) should be defined with negative reward
- There are improperly cited works such as “Duan” and “Schulman”
- Some of the formatting is incorrectly spaced such as in page 3.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents some interesting ideas for the lifelong or multi-tasking RL setting motivated by PAC-Bayes bounds. Despite this, I feel it has some shortcomings in experiments, theory, and clarity as discussed above. Furthermore, the lifelong aspect seems to be overstated and I believe related work insufficiently distinguishes the proposed methods from existing approaches in multi-task and meta RL.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper works in the setting introduced previously by Majumdar et al. 2021 in which a PAC-Bayes formulation of (lifelong) RL was proposed: in direct analogy to supervised learning, a new MDP (given by a simulator) is an example, the policy is the hypothesis used for labeling, and the cost incurred by the policy in the MDP is the loss. PAC-Bayes generalization bounds are then used to obtain loss bounds for i.i.d. MDPs relative to some prior on policies. These generalization bounds are used as an objective function to identify a Gaussian distribution over policies minimizing the bound. A policy sampled from that distribution is then used as an initial policy in a new task, which is in turn fine-tuned on the task with some off-the-shelf learning algorithm.

In the present work, this scheme is modified by periodically updating the prior in the PAC-Bayes bound by mixing the current minimizer of the bound with the prior. The scheme is compared to MAML and single-task learning on some benchmark task families.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strength of the work is that the prior-updating method wasn't considered in this context previously.

There are several significant weaknesses. First, I have some concerns about the experiments. The text says that MAML was given the same number of steps before updating "for fairness," but based on the study of the effect of the updating frequency, it looks like this was essentially optimized for the method presented here, where the data in the plots shows that performance of the method is often sensitive to the frequency. Unless MAML is also optimized by this choice, that does not seem fair at all. 

Second, moreover, I don't understand why the method of Majumdar et al. is not included as a baseline. The text says that it cannot be used in lifelong learning, but that seems wrong -- as far as I can tell, the setting is largely identical, and I think this substantially misrepresents the relationship to Majumdar et al. I would thus want to be provided with a sense of how much the performance is due to the novel element of the present work, relative to the previous work.

Third, the theoretical guarantees seem very close to those provided by Majumdar et al., to the extent that I have trouble assessing any improvement due to the new method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work is hard to follow from the text at a few important points, particularly the description of the new method. The description of the setting also obscures the fact that the MDP M_i is given as a simulator (which although common in the past, is a somewhat serious restriction shared with the work by Majumdar et al., relative to other current works on lifelong learning in RL).

As mentioned in the previous section, the novelty seems somewhat minimal -- the prior-update method is new, but everything else seems nearly identical to Majumdar et al, and no direct comparison to what one would obtain with their method is included.
content.summary_of_the_review: The technical contribution, relative to prior work, seems slight. The paper misrepresents its relationship to the prior work by Majumdar et al. 2021 that is clearly the starting point of this work. The theoretical guarantees seem to be the same and the experiments omit any comparison to that method. The experiments are also a bit fishy in the use of the same update-frequency for MAML and the proposed method, where this parameter seems to be optimized in favor of the proposed method. Thus it isn't clear whether or not the proposed method represents a real advance in the state of the art.

content.title: Few-shot Lifelong Reinforcement Learning with Generalization Guarantees: An Empirical PAC-Bayes Approach
content.abstract: We propose a new empirical PAC-Bayes approach to develop lifelong reinforcement learning algorithms with theoretical guarantees. The main idea is to extend the PAC-Bayes theory in supervised learning to the reinforcement learning regime. More specifically, we train a distribution of policies, and gradually improve the distribution parameters via optimizing the generalization error bound using trajectories from each task. As the agent sees more tasks, it elicits better prior distributions of policies, resulting in tighter generalization bounds and improved future learning. To demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to recent state-of-the-art methods, we test the proposed algorithms on various OpenAI's Gym and Mujuco environments and show that they adapt to new tasks more efficiently by continuously distilling knowledge from past tasks.
